## The question

I still ask an assistant to write the measure. A formula comes back and the report runs. I treat that calculation as a decision, even though nobody has written down how the number is allowed to behave.

[Understanding DAX contracts when using AI](https://www.sqlbi.com/tv/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) is Alberto Ferrari's note from this week. I did not watch the video. I read the [article](https://www.sqlbi.com/articles/understanding-dax-contracts-when-using-ai/) he and Marco Russo published beside it on 5 October 2026. Their example ranks customers in DAX, the formula language in Power BI, Microsoft's reporting product. The page is the claim I am taking from that example. They call the page a contract: a short text that says how a model is allowed to compute. The formula is written after it. The semantic model, the layer under the report where the measures live, is supposed to follow the page.

## The issue

The issue is a formula that runs while the rule was never written down. The meeting then treats the number as agreed.

That is how I slip. I open an assistant, ask for the measure, and review the formula. If it calculates, I move on. Which filters count, and what a total is allowed to show, stay inside the formula. A colleague who wants to argue has to read DAX.

Reports I inherit show the same issue after the meeting is gone. Someone could state the rule in the room, the write-up was skipped, and months later the measure is the only copy left. Russo and Ferrari describe that habit across years of business intelligence, including self-service BI, where the person who knew the business also built the model and the rule still ended inside the formula. Their history is their account. What I have opened matches the ending: one person can parse the measure, and everyone else trusts the tile.

An assistant shortens my path to that ending. A working formula feels finished, so the page never gets written. The next question about the number has nowhere to go except back into the formula. So does the next change in the rule.

## How I keep it from happening again

I already run this gate on Orbit, the public site where an essay like this is published. An assistant may write the draft, and publishing stays a separate action that I take in Slack, so the draft is not the essay until I approve it. Generated text can look finished and still have to wait.

A measure I will defend uses that same split, with a page beside the model in place of the Slack approval. The assistant may write the formula. The formula stays out of the model until the page says which filters change the number, and what a total means when the row is more than one thing. I read the wording the assistant stored, because those sentences will differ from the ones I typed, and then I explain one result out loud from the page alone. If I need the formula to finish that sentence, the measure stays out.

The next change uses the same order: I edit the page first, and the formula waits until the page already says the new rule. When the formula moves and the page stays behind, the written rule and the calculation have split, and the issue is back.

Two limits stay on the gate. While I am still searching for the question, I mark the page as a sketch, and a running formula does not clear that mark. A clear page can also describe the wrong rule. Russo and Ferrari close by saying that, to their knowledge so far, a contract has no drawbacks, yet the assistant will follow a wrong page without argument. The page puts the rule where a colleague can read it, and it still does not choose the rule. I have not done this read-back on a model I maintain, so the assistant's rewrite stays unchecked until I do.

## Takeaway

The issue is a formula that runs while the rule was never written down. The formula stays out until a short page can explain one result, and I change that page before I change the formula.
